first.rationale: The two measured deficits this quarter are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so fixing it plausibly addresses both with one slot. memory_86 and memory_31 both point here, which is why I am spending the single verification pull on memory_86: it is the load-bearing claim for my chosen action, and as a consolidated summary it has lost the details I actually need (effect size, segment, durability window, whether the lift persisted past first week, and what was removed from the flow). memory_31 is 64 days old and SMB-only, so it corroborates but cannot substitute. I deliberately did not choose promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 reports acquisition and revenue lift but the summary is silent on retention, margin, and cohort quality, and discount-led acquisition is the classic way to hit short-term revenue while degrading sustainable qualified revenue — the primary objective here. Matching a price war is also the move that is hardest to reverse once the market has anchored. Downstream value risk is flagged for my own pick as well: memory_31's mechanism was cutting required signup fields, and those fields often carry firmographic data used for lead qualification and enterprise routing (memory_44's sales-assisted path depends on identifying enterprise prospects). Simplifying onboarding could therefore raise raw activation while lowering qualified pipeline, which would look like a win on the headline metric and a loss on the actual objective. So I will run this as a standard experiment with segment-split measurement, tracking not just completion and week-one activation but lead-qualification completeness, enterprise routing rate, and 30-day retention, and I will not treat an activation lift alone as success. If the archived record for memory_86 shows the original lift was small, short-lived, or confined to a segment that is not the one currently declining, I will downgrade to a small guarded test or reconsider activation_messaging (memory_91) as the cheaper in-product lever.

final.rationale:
The archive confirms memory_86 on its own terms and strengthens it beyond what the consolidated summary carried: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and — importantly — 30-day retention +3%. That retention figure is the one I most needed, because it is the difference between a flow change that inflates a funnel metric and one that produces accounts that stay. It also directly answers my main worry about the objective: this is a lever that moved durable behavior, not just a headline number. Combined with memory_31's independent SMB signal, I am committing to simplify_onboarding for this week's slot. The fit to the situation is the reason I am not diverting to the competitor's pricing move: onboarding completion is down 4% and activation is down 6%, onboarding sits upstream of activation, and exp_86 shows this lever moves completion, speed-to-value, and retention together. Promotional pricing (memory_73) remains the tempting response to the competitor, but that memory reports only acquisition and revenue lift and stays silent on retention, margin, and cohort quality — exactly the dimensions the primary objective is written in — and a price response is the hardest move to unwind once the market anchors on it. Meeting a price attack with faster time-to-value is the more defensible answer.

Uncertainty I am carrying rather than resolving: exp_86's record does not say which segment it ran in, over what window, or what specifically was removed from the flow. memory_31's mechanism was cutting required signup fields, and if I reach for that same mechanism I risk stripping firmographic data that feeds lead qualification and the enterprise routing that memory_44 depends on. That is the live downstream-value risk, and the archive did not clear it. So the experiment removes friction from onboarding steps rather than deleting qualification fields wherever the two can be separated; where a field must go, it moves to post-activation capture instead of vanishing. Standard experiment, not broad rollout, because the confirmed effect came from one prior context and the current quarter's decline may have a different cause than the one exp_86 addressed. Success is judged on completion, week-one activation, 30-day retention, and enterprise routing rate plus lead-qualification completeness together; an activation lift paired with a drop in qualified pipeline is a failure, not a win, and I will read it that way.
